turns.q: Is Amazon's earnings quality deteriorating? Put operating cash flow beside net income for the last eight quarters, show the accruals ratio trend, tell me whether receivables and inventory are growing faster than revenue over the same windows, and say what that means for the size of our AMZN position.
turns.answer:
AMZN’s earnings quality does not look like it is deteriorating in the clean sense you asked about. Operating cash flow has remained well above net income across the last eight reported quarters: $25.28B, $25.97B, $45.64B, $17.02B, $32.52B, $35.52B, $54.46B, and $26.03B; net income over the same quarters was $13.48B, $15.33B, $20.00B, $17.13B, $18.16B, $21.19B, $21.19B, and $30.25B.
The accruals ratio trend is also not pointing to deterioration. It was negative throughout and improved through 2025: -3.08%, -10.7%, -10.3%, -9.06%, and -7.56%. That is still a cash-supportive pattern.
On working capital, the picture is mixed but not weak. Receivables are growing faster than revenue in the latest year-over-year comparison: $75.53B versus $54.22B, with receivables growth at 39.3% against revenue growth at 16.6%. Inventory is not showing the same problem: inventory growth slowed from 19.7% to 14.9%, 12.0%, and 1.87%, while revenue growth stayed at 13.3%, 13.4%, 13.6%, and 16.6%. The cash conversion cycle is improving materially, moving from -36.13 to -27.03, -28.70, -35.56, and -51.12.
For the AMZN position in port_001, I could not get citeable concentration-room figures from the limits desk. The desk said "64 more figures were computed and not shown; request fewer names, or name the ones you need", so I cannot state a precise size change from the limit framework. What I can say is that the earnings-quality evidence alone does not justify an automatic cut: cash conversion is still strong, accruals are improving, and inventory is not outrunning revenue. The main caution is receivables, which have started to grow faster than revenue, so I would read this as a watch-closely case rather than a deterioration case that by itself forces a smaller position.

turns.q: Will Lilly's margins keep expanding next year?
turns.answer:
Lilly’s latest net margin rose from 23.5% to 31.7%, so the latest filed trend is still expanding.
But I would not treat that as a forecast that margins will keep expanding next year. The desk does not forecast, and No projected margin figure is held; that absence is policy, not missing data. The filing-based drivers the desk surfaced point both ways: gross margin as a percent of revenue increased versus 2024, mainly from favorable product mix and improved cost of production, partly offset by lower realized prices; at the same time, research and development expenses increased 21 percent in 2025 because of continued investments in the early- and late-stage portfolio, and marketing, selling, and administrative expenses increased 29 percent in 2025 because of promotional efforts supporting launches.
So my read is: the recent direction supports margin expansion, but next year’s expansion is not something the desk will project, and the filing drivers show meaningful offsetting cost pressure. Gross and operating margin were not measurable from the filed lines here, so only net margin is settled.
